analysis.one_liner: Restores strict federal oversight of mid-sized banks by repealing the 2018 deregulation law.
analysis.headline: The SVB Act, written after Silicon Valley Bank's failure, drew 68 Democratic cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote in the House Financial Services Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: After Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in March 2023, this bill would have undone Title IV of the 2018 law that loosened bank rules. It would drop the asset threshold for mandatory strict oversight from $250 billion to $50 billion, forcing mid-sized banks back under stress tests, liquidity requirements, leverage limits, and 'living will' plans for winding down safely [S2] [S3]. It also tightens stress-testing requirements for banks as small as $10 billion in assets and requires risk committees at banks over $10 billion [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Bank customers, depositors, and taxpayers. Stricter oversight of mid-sized banks is meant to prevent the kind of failure that saw SVB's uninsured depositors rescued only through emergency government action, with costs spread across the banking system and backed ultimately by the federal safety net [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Requires banks with $50 billion to $250 billion in assets to comply with enhanced prudential standards again: stress testing, leverage limits, liquidity requirements, and resolution ('living will') plans [S2] [S3].
Expands stress testing by requiring company-run stress tests at banks down to $10 billion in assets, performed annually or semiannually, and raises board-run scenarios from two to three [S2].
Restores the mandatory risk-committee requirement at banks with assets above $10 billion instead of $50 billion [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Regional and mid-sized banks (roughly $10 billion to $250 billion in assets), which would bear the compliance costs of regular stress tests, tighter liquidity rules, and resolution planning. Some of that cost could be passed to borrowers or depositors through fees and rates.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on regional banks, which have argued that one-size-fits-all rules push customers and business toward the largest banks, increasing concentration in banking. (General knowledge about how bank compliance costs scale; not in the sources.)

Under current law the Federal Reserve already has discretion to apply enhanced standards to banks between $100 billion and $250 billion, so a good-faith objection is that supervisor judgment, not the statutory threshold, failed at SVB — meaning the fix targets the 2018 law rather than the regulators who did not act [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — reducing the chance that a mid-sized bank failure again forces emergency government support — is broad and preventive, but hard to price. The cost, borne by mid-sized banks, is real compliance expense. This is a deliberate trade: the bill chooses stricter rules over lighter ones in exchange for a safer system.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the SVB Act on March 14, 2023, days after Silicon Valley Bank's failure, to repeal the 2018 deregulation that raised the threshold for strict bank oversight [S1] [S3].
Sixty-eight House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored [S4].
The House referred the bill to the Financial Services Committee on March 14, 2023, and no further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever taken [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill advancing, so the 2018 rules for mid-sized banks remained in place [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mid-sized and regional banks that operate under the lighter rules enacted in 2018 kept that treatment, avoiding the compliance costs the bill would have imposed. Bank shareholders also avoided the additional capital and liquidity constraints the bill would have restored.

for.name: Katie Porter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SVB Act to repeal the 2018 bank deregulation following the SVB collapse.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled [S5].

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 224 House Republicans sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-run committee did not advance it.

sides.party_line_note: All 68 cosponsors were House Democrats and none of the 224 House Republicans signed on; the Republican-majority Financial Services Committee took no action on the bill [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Regional and mid-sized banks ($50B–$250B in assets)
industries.note: The bill would have stripped the lighter 2018 rules these banks received and put them back under stress tests, liquidity requirements, and resolution planning. Its interest in keeping lighter rules runs against the public's interest in bank stability, since these lighter rules are what the bill was written to reverse after SVB's failure [S2].
Would face new company-run stress tests and risk-committee requirements at the $10 billion threshold [S2].
The bill revises the supplemental leverage ratio applied to custodial banks, changing their capital treatment in ways that cut both ways [S2].
